solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Beard perhaps dad cut back for picture (4,7)

indicators.note: to send something back is to return it the way it came, so SNIP is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: Mary Beard, the classicist and broadcaster, is one Beard

annotation.surface: A father trims his beard short before a photograph.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beard perhaps' looks like facial hair, but it is a surname: the 'perhaps' warns you that Mary is just one Beard.
annotation.definitionFit: Picture in the old sense of a film, as in 'going to the pictures'; the 1964 Disney musical is the example.

entries.clue: Worn-out parent briefly advanced and lifted bag (4-5)

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short, so MOTHER loses its last letter
in a down clue, raising a word turns it upside down, so NET reads upwards

blocks.note: MOTHER with its last letter dropped
A = advanced, as in A level
to net = to bag, to catch

annotation.surface: An exhausted parent hauls a bag up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bag' is a verb here, as in bagging a catch; lifted in a down clue it reads upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative use: cloth chewed by moths is shabby, so anything tired and outdated is called moth-eaten.

entries.clue: Delivers secure buckles, having checked Sierra (7)

indicators.note: a thing that buckles bends out of shape, so the letters of SECURE lose their order
a checked bag is taken in, so the mix takes in S as well

blocks.note: Sierra is S in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Someone fastens buckles after checking on a mountain range.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Buckles' looks like a noun, the fastenings; it is a verb, meaning bends out of shape.
annotation.definitionFit: The biblical sense of deliver, as in 'deliver us from evil': to save from danger.

entries.clue: Food from Beatles bandleader on island (9)

blocks.note: Sgt Pepper leads the Lonely Hearts Club Band on the Beatles album

annotation.surface: A Beatle's snack while holidaying on an island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beatles bandleader' suggests Lennon or McCartney, but it is the fictional Sgt Pepper.
annotation.definitionFit: A broad category standing for one example: the spicy Italian-American salami found on pizzas.

entries.clue: Questions some youngsters about end of term (5)

indicators.note: about means around, so PUPS is placed around the M
takes the final letter of term

blocks.note: pups = young animals, or cheeky youngsters

annotation.surface: A teacher quizzes pupils at the end of term.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Questions' is a verb: to pump someone is to question them hard for information.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: to pump someone is to draw information out of them, the way a pump draws up water.

entries.clue: Stunned when “Middle Ages” is broadcast (2,1,4)

indicators.note: broadcasting is heard, not seen, so we go by sound

blocks.note: middle = inner, ages = days (as in 'the old days')

annotation.surface: A dazed viewer watches a programme about medieval history.
annotation.walkthrough: In a British accent, with the R unsounded, 'inner days' is said just like 'in a daze'. The capitals make 'Middle Ages' look like the historical period.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone stunned is dazed, unable to think clearly.

entries.clue: Seat in Orton play’s tipped over (5)

indicators.note: something tipped over ends up the other way round, so LOOTS is written backwards

blocks.note: Loot is a comedy by Joe Orton; with the 's it gives LOOTS

annotation.surface: A chair at a performance of a Joe Orton play gets knocked over.
annotation.walkthrough: Joe Orton was an English playwright of the 1960s, and Loot is his best-known farce. The possessive 's supplies the S.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain category: a stool is one kind of seat, the backless kind.

entries.clue: Strokes cat’s tail in places (5)

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its last letter
one thing in another sits inside it, so T goes into PUTS

annotation.surface: Someone strokes a cat's tail here and there.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Strokes' suggests petting the cat; in golf a putt is a stroke on the green.
annotation.definitionFit: Golf's sense of stroke, one hit of the ball; putts are the gentle ones on the green.

entries.clue: Painter‘s subject, out of sorts, is tense (11)

blocks.note: the point = the subject under discussion

annotation.surface: An artist's model feels unwell and anxious.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of sorts' looks like an anagram signal, but it simply means ILL.
annotation.definitionFit: A kind of painter, like Seurat, who builds pictures from small dots of colour.

entries.clue: Soft old politician with a grim hairstyle (9)

annotation.surface: A gentle, aged politician sports an unfortunate haircut.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A grim hairstyle' reads as one phrase, but 'with' is the link and 'hairstyle' stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: One named style, hair swept up high from the forehead, called after Madame de Pompadour.

entries.clue: Bit of kit that lock’s put on? (5,6)

annotation.definition: Bit of kit that lock’s put on?

blocks.note: sounds like a gadget or tool; it is a piece of sports clothing
read as a curl of hair or a door fitting; a lock is a second-row forward in rugby, pulling on his shirt

annotation.surface: A curl of hair has had a piece of equipment fitted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lock' suggests hair or a door, but in rugby a lock is a forward, and his jersey is the kit he puts on.
annotation.definitionFit: Kit is British for sports clothing, and the jersey is the shirt a rugby lock wears.

entries.clue: Chilling thing with six faces … (3,4)

blocks.note: read as something scary, a horror; meant literally as something that makes a drink cold
sounds like a many-headed monster; a cube has six flat faces

annotation.surface: Something scary with six faces, like a monster.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins it to the next clue, keeping the horror going, but the two are solved separately.
annotation.definitionFit: Literal twice over: ice chills, and a cube is the solid with six square faces.

entries.clue: … creature‘s weird legs start to approach us (3,4)

indicators.note: something weird is out of the usual shape, so the letters are rearranged
takes the first letter of approach

annotation.surface: A monster with strange legs begins to close in on us, following the chilling thing before it.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the horror film on from 10 across, though the two clues are independent.
annotation.definitionFit: A broad category for one example: a soft-bodied marine mollusc without a shell.

entries.clue: Children grabbing second of teddy bears (5)

indicators.note: to grab something is to take hold of it, so TOTS closes around the E
takes the second letter of teddy

annotation.surface: Children snatch at teddy bears.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Teddy bears' reads as one toy, but 'bears' is the verb definition: carries.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb sense of bear, to carry; to tote is informal for carrying something about.

entries.clue: Befuddled once by mist when leaving motorway, curse? (9)

indicators.note: a befuddled mind is muddled, so the letters are mixed up
what leaves goes out, so M is taken from the letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, before the M is removed
M = motorway, as in the M1; this letter is removed

annotation.surface: A driver, confused by fog on coming off the motorway, swears.
annotation.walkthrough: Remove the M from ONCE BY MIST and rearrange the nine letters left.
annotation.definitionFit: The noun sense of curse, a swear word, rather than a spell cast on someone.

entries.clue: Flower from Spooner’s unwanted plant patch (9)

indicators.note: swap the opening sounds of the two words, as Rev Spooner did

blocks.note: unwanted plant = weed, patch = spell (a period); swap W and SP

annotation.surface: A gardener's flower growing in a weedy patch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Patch' means a spell of time, as in a bad patch, not a piece of ground.
annotation.definitionFit: A category for one example: speedwell is a small blue wild flower.

entries.clue: Employed popular head to entertain half of Harrow (2,7)

indicators.note: a host entertains guests inside the house, so the outer letters hold HAR
takes the first half of Harrow

blocks.note: a ness is a headland, as in Dungeness

annotation.surface: A well-liked headmaster hosts pupils from Harrow, the English public school.
annotation.walkthrough: Harrow is a famous English boarding school, which makes 'head' look like a headteacher; it is a headland. 'Popular head' together forms the host.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: a horse in harness is at work, so a person in harness is employed.

entries.clue: Possibly one left with the cumin for cooking (9)

indicators.note: food that is cooked is stirred and mixed, so the letters are mixed up

annotation.surface: A recipe where just one lot of cumin is left over to cook with.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One' is a time: one o'clock, and 'possibly' flags that it is only an example.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example turned round: one o'clock is a typical time to eat lunch.

entries.clue: What bowler maybe can hold, stifling England’s opener, nasty (7)

indicators.note: to stifle is to smother, so HATFUL closes over the E
the first letter of England

blocks.note: a bowler is a hat, so what it holds is a hatful

annotation.surface: A cricket bowler can hold out against England's opening batsman, who is unpleasant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bowler' and 'England's opener' are pure cricket; the bowler is a hat.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something hateful is thoroughly unpleasant.

entries.clue: Yellowish-brown ring about to be found outside church (5)

indicators.note: the ring and RE stand outside the church, so they wrap round CH

annotation.surface: A tan-coloured ring is about to turn up outside a church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'going to'; 'about' is RE and 'to be found outside' does the placing.
annotation.definitionFit: A colour name taken from the earth pigment used by painters since prehistory.

entries.clue: Hallowe’en celebrations finish me off? (7)

blocks.note: sound like a party that wears you out; they fall on the 31st, the last day of the month
read as 'exhaust me'; meant as 'bring me to an end', spoken by the month itself

annotation.surface: Someone worn out by Halloween parties.
annotation.walkthrough: The speaker is the month, not a tired reveller; the question mark flags the trick.
annotation.definitionFit: Hallowe'en, 31 October, is the month's closing day, so it ends October.

entries.clue: Cons discontented Italian couple and son (7)

indicators.note: with its contents gone, ITALIAN keeps only its outer letters

blocks.note: to mate = to couple, pair up

annotation.surface: Unhappy Italian parents and their son, perhaps swindlers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Couple' is a verb here, MATE, rather than a pair of people.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang: a con is short for convict, and convicts are the inmates of a prison.

entries.clue: Prophet‘s way of working seems deficient occasionally (5)

indicators.note: lacking letters here and there, so only every other letter of seems is kept

annotation.surface: A prophet's methods appear lacking at times.
annotation.walkthrough: MO is Latin shorthand, modus operandi, for someone's method.
annotation.definitionFit: A category for one example: the Old Testament leader who received the Ten Commandments.

entries.clue: More certain to be found on board pleasure ride (5)

indicators.note: passengers on board are carried inside, so the answer sits within the words that follow

annotation.surface: Someone feels safer on a boat trip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a ship; it means carried inside the letters of pleasure ride.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the comparative: sure is certain, so surer is more certain.

entries.clue: People excessively fond of star, odd eccentric (7)

indicators.note: an eccentric strays from the normal pattern, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Fans obsessed with a strange, oddball celebrity.
annotation.walkthrough: The fans in the surface are a red herring: the definition leans on an old dictionary sense.
annotation.definitionFit: An older dictionary sense: a dotard is one who dotes; today it usually means a senile old person.

entries.clue: Group of workers drilling pavement ask for cement (4,5)

indicators.note: a drill bores through material, so the answer bores through the words that follow

annotation.surface: Road workers digging up a pavement ask for cement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Group of workers drilling' reads as a road crew; 'drilling' is the signal that the answer runs through the next words.
annotation.definitionFit: A task force is a team put together for one particular job.

entries.clue: Muscular honey manufacturer cleared out factory (5)

indicators.note: a room cleared out is emptied, so factory loses its middle and keeps F and Y

annotation.surface: A strong honey producer has emptied its factory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Honey manufacturer' sounds like a company, but it is the insect.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal: beef is muscle, so someone beefy is heavily built.

entries.clue: The Sun features very large American Republican with wide trousers (5,6)

blocks.note: flares are trousers that widen below the knee

annotation.surface: A tabloid story about a big American Republican in baggy trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper, so 'The Sun features' reads as its articles; here it is the star.
annotation.definitionFit: Features in the sense of characteristic parts: bright eruptions on the star's surface.
